issues.title: Internal distributor failure causing stalling, no-start, and misfires
issues.description:
The TEC/Hitachi internal-coil distributor on third-generation Integras is a chronic failure point. Heat from the internal ignition coil degrades the coil, igniter (ICM), and bearings, causing intermittent stalling at operating temperature, hot-restart problems, and dead no-starts. 
The 1996 Acura Integra has the most overall complaints, with the most-reported problem being distributor failure. This issue can cause difficulty starting the car, stalling, and misfiring.
 
The car has been in the shop because the driver was driving and it just shut off with no warning or light. Come to find out it was the distributor so they changed it.
issues.solution:
Pull DTCs first — codes P1381 (cylinder position sensor) and Code 22 commonly originate inside the distributor. 
P1381 is the cylinder position sensor code, located inside the distributor.
 Replace the complete OEM distributor assembly (avoid cheap aftermarket — many fail within months). OBD1 (94-95) and OBD2 (96-99) distributors are not interchangeable. 
It is worth noting that the distributor plugs are different for each obd generation. So the obd1, and obd2 have different harness plugs.
 Budget $250-550 for a quality unit installed.

citations.title: Anatomy of a B-series Distributor — Team Integra Forums
Acura Integra - distributor, no start (SOLVED) - Car Talk Community
Acura Integra problems and complaints — Slotcar Today

communityRecommendations.content: Use a genuine Honda/Hitachi OEM distributor — aftermarket re-mans commonly fail again within months.
Mark the distributor housing position before removal so you can return to base timing without a timing light.

issues.title: Distributor O-ring leaks oil onto transmission bellhousing
issues.description:
The O-ring sealing the distributor shaft to the cylinder head shrinks and hardens, allowing oil to weep out behind the distributor and run down the back of the head onto the top of the transmission. Owners often misdiagnose it as a head gasket or cam seal leak. 
Owners report a problem with the b18b1 head leaking oil where the distributor plugs into the head, with the little o-ring gasket being the cause.
 
Owners notice their GSR a little low on oil, with the leak coming from behind the dizzy, and oil on the coolant temp sensor.
issues.solution:
Remove the three distributor mounting bolts, pull the distributor (mark its position first), and replace the O-ring with an OEM Honda part (~$5). 
There is an O-ring around the distributor. Take the three bolts off that hold the unit in, mark the position, there is an O-ring on the part that goes into the engine. Honda sells these for like $5.
 If the leak persists, inspect the VTEC solenoid gasket and the rocker shaft freeze plug at the rear of the head — 
it was the vtec rocker shaft freeze plug/seal that was the cause
 in some persistent cases.
symptoms: oil drips on top of transmission
burning oil smell from engine bay

citations.title: distributor oil leak — Team Integra Forums
Bad Distributor Oil Leak — Honda-Tech
Distributor o ring leak...FIXED w/pics — Team Integra Forums

communityRecommendations.content: Replace the VTEC solenoid gasket at the same time — it leaks from the same area and is cheap insurance.
Do not use RTV in place of the O-ring; it will not seal long-term and complicates future removal.

issues.title: Ignition switch contact pitting causes engine to die when key released
issues.description:
The electrical contact block on the steering-column ignition switch develops pitted contacts. The car will crank and start, but as soon as the key returns from START to RUN the contact fails and the engine dies. Sometimes the car will run if the key is held partially toward START. 
Driving home and the 95 Acura Integra 4 door GSR died on the highway. If trying to start the car, it would start then die as the key was released. Holding the key close to III kept the engine on. The ignition harness switching mechanism contact point was pitted.
issues.solution:
Replace the ignition switch electrical portion (not the cylinder/lock) — it unbolts from the back of the steering column lock housing with two screws. OEM Honda part is the most reliable choice. 
The issue is starting the car and it dies as soon as you let go of the key. After research, it became obvious it was an ignition switch issue.
 Check the under-hood main fuse and the ignition fuses before condemning the switch. Budget $50-150 for parts and 1 hour labor.
symptoms: engine dies when key returns to RUN
must hold key toward START to keep running

citations.title: 1995 Acura Integra Electrical System: Ignition: Switch Problems — CarComplaints
Ignition switch issue — Honda-Tech
1996 Acura Integra Ignition Switch Problems — CarComplaints

communityRecommendations.content: Test fuses and the under-hood main fuse first — symptoms can mimic switch failure.
Aftermarket ignition switches are hit-or-miss; the OEM Honda part is worth the price.

issues.title: 4-speed automatic: shift solenoid failure causes D4 light flash, missed shifts, and limp mode
issues.description:
The Honda BAXA/MAXA 4-speed automatic in the Integra is notoriously sensitive to fluid condition and shift-solenoid contamination. Solenoid A/B failure causes flashing D4 light, harsh or missed 2-3/3-4 shifts, loss of power in D4/D3, and sometimes speedometer drop-out. 
Integra often faces delayed or missed shifts and manual downshifting difficulties in automatic transmissions. Shifting problems in the 1998 Integra's automatic transmission can stem from a clogged transmission filter or screen restricting fluid flow. This causes poor hydraulic pressure, leading to missed 4th gear shifts and failure to downshift.
 
While driving, the D4 suddenly lost almost all power, wouldn't shift, and the speedometer stopped working. Codes returned were Automatic Transaxle FI A circuit failure and ELD error.
issues.solution:
Drain-and-fill with Honda ATF-Z1/DW-1 (NEVER use generic Dexron — it will destroy the clutches). 
The transmission fluid in the Integra 4AT's are supposed to be changed every 3 years/36,000 mi. It can cook and wear out just like the oil in your engine.
 Pull codes with a Honda jumper or scan tool; the lock-up and shift solenoids are external, three-bolt parts accessible from the engine bay and often just need cleaning. 
A screwed up lock-up solenoid will give you a general CEL #70 (Automatic Transaxle); the solenoid is totally accessible from the engine bay and costs less than $200 to replace. It's held in place by three bolts.

citations.title: Auto transmission B18B1 won't move car — Team Integra
99 Integra Transmission Problem — Acura World
Auto transmission issue (ATF service guide) — Team Integra

communityRecommendations.content: Use only Honda ATF-Z1 or DW-1. Generic ATF causes shift flare and premature failure.
Pull the specific solenoid code before condemning the transmission — a $150 solenoid often fixes it.

issues.title: Timing belt failure on interference B18 engine bends valves
issues.description:
All B18 engines in the 94-99 Integra are interference-design. If the timing belt snaps (or jumps teeth from a seized tensioner or water pump), pistons strike open valves. The belt should be replaced every 90,000 miles along with the water pump, tensioner, and seals. 
The timing belt in the DOHC Honda engine keeps engine running and valvetrain events on time. Because the 1.8 liter B18 engine is an interference engine, failure of the timing belt usually means pistons have hit valves. This can lead to lack of cylinder compression at the bare minimum. At worst the valve may become stuck or destroy the piston.
issues.solution:
Replace the complete timing belt kit: belt (125T non-VTEC, 126T VTEC), tensioner, tensioner spring, water pump, cam and crank seals, and balance shaft belt where applicable. 
Timing belt part numbers are 14400-P7J-004 or 14400-PR4-A01 for the 19-tooth LS water pump, with water pump 19200-P75-003 or 19200-PT5-000.
 Do NOT mix LS and GSR water pumps — the tooth counts differ. 
The water pumps are not the same. They have different amounts of teeth on them.
 Professional cost: 
in the ballpark of 350-600 dollars for a job of this type
.

citations.title: How To Change a B18B Timing Belt — My Pro Street
How To Change Your B18C1 DOHC VTEC Timing Belt — My Pro Street
Acura Integra Timing Belt — PartsGeek

communityRecommendations.content: Use a Japanese-made kit (Aisin water pump, Mitsuboshi or Gates belt) — avoid no-name kits.
Replace at 90k miles or 7 years even if the belt looks fine; tensioner bearings seize without warning.

issues.title: VTEC oil pressure switch failure (Code 22 / P1259) on GS-R and Type R
issues.description:
The VTEC oil pressure switch screwed into the VTEC solenoid assembly on B18C engines fails or leaks, triggering CEL with OBD1 Code 22 or OBD2 P1259. Symptoms include VTEC not engaging at high RPM and a hard rev-limiter drop. 
Owner had a 99 GSR with CEL constantly on and code 22 (VTEC Oil Pressure Switch). Even after replacing it with a new one and swapping the VTEC solenoid, the problem occurred after going into VTEC and letting off, mostly around 60-90mph.
 
Error code 22 corresponds to the front valve timing oil pressure switch, which is the VTEC oil pressure switch.
issues.solution:
Verify oil level and condition first — 
if the code is still present after checking, make sure there is plenty of oil and then reset the ECU
. The switch is the green-plug sensor on top of the VTEC solenoid; replace with OEM Honda part. 
Replace the switch. It's the green plug located on the vtec solenoid.
 If the code returns after replacement, install a mechanical oil pressure gauge — 
a worn oil pump or internal leak can cause low pressure that triggers the code; an oil pressure gauge will confirm
. Switch is ~$70 OEM.

citations.title: VTEC Oil Pressure Switch Code 22 help! — Team Integra
VTEC Oil Pressure Switch Problem — Team Integra
Error code 22 on Integra GSR! — Tampa Racing

communityRecommendations.content: Do an oil and filter change before replacing the switch — gunked oil galleries often cause the same code.
Aftermarket VTEC controllers commonly trigger this code by changing the engagement RPM the ECU expects.

issues.title: Rear lower control arm bolts seize and shear inside bushing sleeves
issues.description:
The long bolts that pass through the rear lower control arm inner bushings corrode to the steel sleeve inside the bushing. Any attempt to remove them for alignment, bushing, or shock work results in a sheared bolt and a destroyed bushing sleeve. This is a near-universal complaint in rust-belt cars. 
Owners had to cut the ears that go around the LCA off the strut because the bolts rust to the inside of the bushing.
 
LCA bolts break ALL the time.
issues.solution:
Soak bolts with penetrating fluid (PB Blaster/Kroil) for days before attempting removal; heat the bushing sleeve with a torch. If the bolt shears, the only fix is to cut the bushing out and drill/punch the remaining sleeve from the subframe ear. 
When you are down there and replacing rusted bolts, if they are rusted on bad enough you might have to break the welded nut they go into on the front side of the subframe and trailing arms. You can get matching sized nuts and washers.
 Replace with OEM Honda bolts (M10x1.25, ~$4-9 each from the dealer). 
Diameter = 10mm, Pitch = 1.25.

citations.title: Lower Control Arm Bolt Replacement — Team Integra
Rear Lower control arm bolt? — Team Integra

communityRecommendations.content: Spray penetrating oil into the bushing sleeve through both ends a week before the job.
Use proper-grade OEM bolts — hardware-store bolts are not always the correct grade for this safety-critical joint.

issues.title: Cable-style power window regulator frays and window falls into door
issues.description:
The factory cable-driven window regulator frays inside the spool housing. The window then moves slowly, gets stuck, makes grinding or clicking noise, or drops into the door. The driver's door is most commonly affected due to use frequency. 
An inoperative power window would commonly be caused by failure of the cable in the window regulator, or the window motor itself. The window regulator will need to be replaced as an assembly to correct this concern.
 
A clicking, chattering, or grinding noise when the window moves can indicate a failing regulator. In some cases a severely damaged window regulator could cause the window to drop inside the door.
issues.solution:
Replace the regulator assembly — the cable cannot be serviced separately. Remove door panel, lower glass to expose the two regulator-to-glass bolts, then six bolts holding regulator to door shell. 
Disconnect the 6 bolts holding the window regulator to the door. Remove regulator/motor assembly through the largest hole in the door.
 Test the motor before condemning — switches and the master switch power module also fail. Total cost: 
starting from $364
 at a shop; DIY parts run $60-150.
symptoms: motor hums but no glass movement

citations.title: Acura Integra Window Won't Go Up or Down — RepairPal

communityRecommendations.content: Test the motor on the bench with battery jumpers before buying a regulator — sometimes only the switch is bad.
Genuine Honda regulators last far longer than budget aftermarket; junkyard OEM is often the best value.
